transmission-line.name: Transmission lines and impedance matching
transmission-line.description: Check characteristic impedance, reflection coefficient, VSWR, return loss, quarter-wave transformers, stubs and reading the Smith chart with multiple-choice questions. The explanations walk through each calculation and the points where it is easy to go wrong.
transmission-line.intro:
At high frequencies the length of a wire can no longer be ignored compared with the wavelength, so the wiring is treated as a transmission line with a characteristic impedance Z0. When the load differs from Z0, a reflection occurs, and its size is given by the reflection coefficient Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0). VSWR and return loss express the same amount of reflection in other forms.
On a line terminated in a mismatched load, the input impedance changes with the length of the line. A quarter-wave line transforms an impedance into its inverse, and short-circuited or open-circuited stubs act as reactive elements. The Smith chart is a tool that shows these changes as movement around a circle.

s-params.name: S-parameters and passive components
s-params.description: Learn the meaning of S11 and S21 and their dB values, insertion loss, the conditions for reciprocity and losslessness, directional couplers, Wilkinson dividers, circulators, ABCD matrices, and L-network matching and Q with multiple-choice questions.
s-params.intro:
RF circuits are described by S-parameters, the ratios of the waves leaving and entering each port. S11 is the input reflection and S21 is the transmission; both are amplitude ratios, so 20 log is used to convert them to dB. A passive circuit containing no magnetic materials is reciprocal, with S21 = S12, and if it is lossless, the reflected and transmitted powers add up to 1.
Passive components such as directional couplers, Wilkinson dividers and circulators are used to monitor transmitter output, split power, and separate transmit from receive. Cascaded circuits are found from the product of their ABCD matrices, and in L-networks and other matching circuits, remember that the circuit Q sets the bandwidth.

microwave.name: Waveguides and microwave components
microwave.description: Check the cutoff frequency and TE10 mode of rectangular waveguides, guide wavelength, cavity resonators, higher-order modes in coaxial lines, isolators, microwave power measurement and PIN diode switches with multiple-choice questions.
microwave.intro:
Above a few GHz, the loss and higher-order modes of coaxial lines become a problem, and waveguides — hollow metal pipes — are used instead. The fundamental mode of a rectangular waveguide is TE10, and frequencies below fc = c/(2a), where the broad dimension a is half a wavelength, do not propagate. The guide wavelength is longer than the free-space wavelength, the phase velocity exceeds the speed of light, and the group velocity is slower than light.
A cavity resonator, made by closing both ends of a waveguide, serves as a high-Q resonator in filters and frequency standards. A ferrite isolator protects an oscillator from reflections from the load, and a PIN diode acts as a switch whose resistance is set by the bias current. In power measurement, the difference between thermal sensors and diode-detector sensors matters.

rf-circuits.name: Noise and nonlinearity
rf-circuits.description: Check thermal noise kTB and −174 dBm/Hz, noise figure and noise temperature, the Friis formula, P1dB, IP3 and intermodulation, dynamic range, image frequency and phase noise with multiple-choice questions.
rf-circuits.intro:
The weakest signal a receiver can pick up is set by noise. Thermal noise power is kTB, which at 290 K is −174 dBm per hertz. The noise added by amplifiers and other stages is expressed as noise figure or noise temperature, and the value for a whole multistage chain is found with the Friis formula. The key point is that the noise figure and gain of the first stage largely set the total.
The strong-signal side is limited by nonlinearity. Typical measures are P1dB, where the gain has dropped by 1 dB, and IP3, which expresses the size of third-order intermodulation; IM3 rises with a slope of 3 dB per 1 dB of input. The image frequency of the mixer and the phase noise of the local oscillator also affect receiver performance.

filters-oscillators.name: Filters, oscillators and PLLs
filters-oscillators.description: Learn the resonant frequency of LC circuits, Q and bandwidth, Butterworth, Chebyshev and Bessel responses, oscillation conditions, quartz crystals, VCOs and varactors, and PLL division ratios and phase noise with multiple-choice questions.
filters-oscillators.intro:
The resonant frequency of an LC circuit is f = 1/(2π√LC), and Q is the center frequency divided by the 3 dB bandwidth. Filters come in responses such as Butterworth, with a flat passband; Chebyshev, which allows ripple for a steeper rolloff; and Bessel, with nearly constant group delay. The choice depends on the application.
An oscillator keeps oscillating under the condition of a loop gain of 1 and a phase of 0°. A quartz crystal stabilizes the frequency with its high Q, and a VCO changes frequency through the capacitance of a varactor. A PLL divides the VCO output and compares it with a reference, producing any frequency with the stability of the reference. The relation between the division ratio and phase noise is also important.

antenna.name: Antennas and propagation
antenna.description: Check half-wave dipoles, dBi and dBd, gain and directivity, effective aperture, free-space path loss and the Friis transmission equation, polarization, Fresnel zones and the radar equation with multiple-choice questions.
antenna.intro:
Antenna gain expresses how much power an antenna can concentrate in a particular direction, relative to an isotropic antenna (dBi) or a half-wave dipole (dBd). A half-wave dipole has a radiation resistance of about 73 Ω and a gain of 2.15 dBi. Gain and effective aperture are linked by Ae = Gλ²/4π.
In free space the received power is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, and the Friis transmission equation lets you estimate the received power of a link. In real propagation, polarization mismatch, obstacles in the Fresnel zone and diffraction add loss. In radar, where the wave travels to the target and back, the received power is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the distance.

modulation.name: Modulation and digital radio
modulation.description: Learn the basics of AM, FM and PM, bits per symbol in PSK and QAM, symbol rate and roll-off, Eb/N0 and SNR, Gray coding, EVM, OFDM and the Shannon limit with multiple-choice questions.
modulation.intro:
In analog modulation, information is carried on the amplitude (AM), frequency (FM) or phase (PM) of a carrier. The power split in AM and the bandwidth of FM (Carson's rule) are basic calculations. In digital modulation, an M-ary scheme sends log₂M bits per symbol, and the bandwidth is set by the symbol rate and the roll-off factor.
Schemes are compared by Eb/N0, normalized to the energy per bit, and bit error rate. The modulation accuracy of a transmitter is expressed as EVM, and OFDM achieves high-speed transmission with many orthogonal subcarriers. Shannon's theorem gives the upper limit on the data rate for a given bandwidth and SNR.

radar.name: Radar and sensing
radar.description: Learn the range resolution and maximum detection range of pulsed radar, Doppler frequency, the beat frequency of FMCW radar, radar cross section, PRF and ambiguous range, angular resolution, and the principles of automotive millimeter-wave radar with multiple-choice questions.
radar.intro:
A radar transmits radio waves, receives the echo from a target, and finds the range from the round-trip delay as R = ct/2. The range resolution of a pulsed radar is cτ/2, set by the pulse width, but with pulse compression it can be made c/(2B), set by the bandwidth B. The pulse repetition frequency (PRF) determines the unambiguous range c/(2·PRF) and the range of velocities that can be measured.
The echo from a moving target has a Doppler frequency of 2v/λ, which gives the radial velocity. Automotive millimeter-wave radars use FMCW, finding range from the beat frequency, velocity from the phase change from chirp to chirp, and angle from the phase differences between multiple receive antennas. How visible a target is to radar is expressed by its radar cross section.

si-emc.name: High-speed signaling and EMC
si-emc.description: Check microstrip and stripline, differential signaling and common mode, crosstalk, rise time and bandwidth, skin effect, TDR, eye diagrams, shielding and decoupling with multiple-choice questions.
si-emc.intro:
Fast digital signals contain high-frequency components set by their rise time (roughly 0.35/tr), so traces on a circuit board are also designed as transmission lines. The basics of the design are the impedance and propagation delay of microstrip and stripline, the differential impedance of differential pairs, and crosstalk with neighboring traces.
At high frequencies the skin effect increases conductor loss, and the return current flows directly beneath the signal trace. Discontinuities in the traces are evaluated with TDR, and signal quality with eye diagrams. On the EMC side, suppressing common-mode current, the material and gaps of shields, and the self-resonance of decoupling capacitors are important.

systems.name: Radio systems and frequencies
systems.description: Learn the ranges of VHF, UHF and SHF and of the L, S, C, X, Ku and Ka bands, wavelength and frequency, EIRP, link margin, noise temperature and G/T, atmospheric and rain attenuation at millimeter waves, and the altitude and delay of geostationary satellites with multiple-choice questions.
systems.intro:
The behavior of radio waves changes greatly with frequency. HF reflects off the ionosphere and reaches great distances, VHF and UHF are used for line-of-sight communication, and SHF and millimeter waves are used for high-capacity communications and radar that take advantage of wide bandwidths and small antennas. At millimeter waves, oxygen absorption and rain attenuation must also be taken into account.
In radio link design, the link margin is found from the transmitter's EIRP, the propagation loss, the receive antenna gain and the receiver sensitivity. In satellite communications, the distance of about 36,000 km to geostationary orbit causes large loss and delay, and the performance of a receiving station is expressed by G/T, the ratio of antenna gain to noise temperature.

measurement.name: RF measurement
measurement.description: Check the RBW and displayed average noise level of spectrum analyzers, VNA error terms and SOLT calibration, power meter zeroing and mismatch uncertainty, the Y-factor method and phase noise measurement with multiple-choice questions.
measurement.intro:
In RF measurement, the noise and distortion of the instrument itself and mismatches in the connections creep into the results. On a spectrum analyzer, the narrower the resolution bandwidth (RBW), the lower the displayed noise level, and the input attenuator setting decides whether noise or distortion takes priority. Signals close to the noise level are read by subtracting the noise contribution in power.
A vector network analyzer (VNA) removes systematic errors such as directivity and source match with SOLT calibration, using short, open, load and thru standards. For power meters, zeroing and mismatch uncertainty are the basics, and for noise figure measurement, the Y-factor method with a noise source. In phase noise measurement, the instrument's own phase noise sets the floor.

power-amp.name: Power amplifiers
power-amp.description: Learn the conduction angle and theoretical efficiency of Class A, B, AB and C, the switching operation of Class D and E, power-added efficiency (PAE), PAPR and output backoff, AM-AM/AM-PM, DPD, load-pull and Doherty amplifiers with multiple-choice questions.
power-amp.intro:
The power amplifier is the circuit that consumes the most power in a transmitter. Classes A, AB, B and C are distinguished by the conduction angle — the part of each input cycle during which current flows — and the narrower the conduction angle, the higher the theoretical efficiency, at the cost of linearity. Classes D and E use the transistor as a switch and ideally reach 100% efficiency. Power-added efficiency (PAE), which subtracts the input power, is also used as a measure of efficiency.
Signals with a high PAPR, such as OFDM, are amplified with output backoff — the average output lowered from saturation so that the peaks are not distorted — which reduces efficiency. AM-AM and AM-PM distortion is corrected with DPD, and efficiency at backoff is raised with the Doherty amplifier, which uses load modulation. The optimum load for large signals is found by load-pull.

phased-array.name: Array antennas and beamforming
phased-array.description: Check the array factor, element spacing and the grating-lobe condition, beamwidth and number of elements, scanning with phase shifters, true time delay and beam squint, analog, digital and hybrid beamforming, and array gain with multiple-choice questions.
phased-array.intro:
An array antenna lines up many antenna elements and shapes its radiation pattern through the amplitude and phase given to each element. The overall pattern is the product of the single-element pattern and the array factor, and setting the phase difference between neighboring elements to Δφ = 2πd sinθ/λ points the beam in the direction θ. If the element spacing is too wide, grating lobes as strong as the main beam appear, so scanning up to an angle θ requires d < λ/(1 + |sinθ|).
With N elements, the S/N improves N times on receive, and on transmit the EIRP grows in proportion to N². Scanning with phase shifters causes beam squint, a shift of beam direction with frequency, so true time delay is used for wideband signals. Depending on where the beam is formed, there are analog schemes that combine at RF, digital schemes that digitize every element, and hybrid schemes that combine the two.

fading.name: Multipath and fading
fading.description: Learn Rayleigh and Rician fading, delay spread and coherence bandwidth, Doppler spread and coherence time, diversity gain, the two-ray model, and path loss exponents and shadowing with multiple-choice questions.
fading.intro:
In mobile communication, radio waves are reflected and scattered by buildings and the ground, and many waves with different delays arrive superimposed. With no direct wave the envelope follows a Rayleigh distribution, and with a strong direct wave it follows a Rician distribution, with deep fades appearing about every half wavelength of movement. The delay spread, the spread of the delays, sets the coherence bandwidth, and the Doppler spread caused by movement sets the coherence time.
In link design, the received level is considered as three parts: the average loss with distance, shadowing from obstruction, and fast fading from multipath. The average loss is expressed by a path loss exponent n, and in the two-ray model, which includes ground reflection, n = 4 at long range. Diversity, which uses several antennas or other branches that fluctuate independently, is effective against deep fades.

receivers.name: Receiver architectures
receivers.description: Check the superheterodyne and image-reject mixers, DC offset and IQ imbalance in zero-IF, low-IF, image rejection ratio, AGC, ADC quantization noise, and receiver sensitivity and blocking with multiple-choice questions.
receivers.intro:
A receiver amplifies the weak signal picked up by the antenna, lowers its frequency and then demodulates it. A superheterodyne converts to a fixed intermediate frequency (IF) and selects the channel with a fixed filter, removing the image 2×IF away from the received frequency with a filter ahead of the mixer or with an image-reject mixer. Direct conversion (zero-IF) converts straight to baseband, so it is easy to integrate, but it suffers from DC offset, IQ imbalance and second-order distortion.
Receiver performance is set on the weak-signal side by sensitivity and on the strong-signal side by distortion and saturation. Sensitivity is found from thermal noise, noise figure and the required S/N, and a strong nearby interferer lowers it through compression and reciprocal mixing (blocking). The S/N of the ADC that finally digitizes the signal is ideally 6.02N + 1.76 dB, and the AGC keeps the level entering the ADC appropriate even as the input strength changes.

matching.name: Impedance matching network design
matching.description: Learn how to calculate L-network element values, the relation between a matching network's Q and bandwidth, π- and T-networks, how elements move a point on the Smith chart, the difference from quarter-wave transformers, conjugate versus noise matching, and the Bode–Fano limit with multiple-choice questions.
matching.intro:
A matching network transforms the load impedance into a value that, seen from the source, receives the maximum power. In an L-network matching two resistances, the shunt element goes on the higher-resistance side, and the Q is fixed by the resistance ratio as Q = √(Rhigh/Rlow − 1). The higher the Q, the narrower the bandwidth, so several L-sections are cascaded for a wider bandwidth, and π- or T-networks are used when the Q should be chosen separately from the resistance ratio (at a value higher than the L-network's).
The Smith chart is a convenient design tool: series elements move the point along constant-resistance circles and shunt elements along constant-conductance circles. Conjugate matching, which gives maximum power, and noise matching, which minimizes the noise figure, generally do not coincide, so an LNA needs a compromise between them. And for loads containing capacitance, the Bode–Fano limit means a perfect match over a wide band is impossible.

ofdm-mimo.name: OFDM and MIMO
ofdm-mimo.description: Check the IFFT and subcarrier spacing in OFDM, cyclic prefix length and efficiency, pilot placement, MIMO spatial multiplexing and stream count, space-time codes, diversity order, and eigenmode transmission with water-filling through multiple-choice questions.
ofdm-mimo.intro:
OFDM divides a wide band into many narrow subcarriers and modulates them all at once with an IFFT. When the subcarrier spacing is the reciprocal of the useful symbol duration they are mutually orthogonal, and adding a cyclic prefix in front of each symbol allows each subcarrier to be equalized with a single complex multiplication even in the presence of delayed waves. The CP length, the subcarrier spacing and the pilot density are chosen by balancing delay spread against Doppler.
MIMO uses multiple antennas at both ends, sending up to min(Nt, Nr) streams on the same frequency at the same time by spatial multiplexing, or obtaining diversity with space-time codes. If the transmitter knows the channel, singular value decomposition splits it into parallel channels, and allocating power by water-filling maximizes capacity. The correlation of the propagation path and the detection method also determine how much gain is obtained.

propagation.name: Radio-wave propagation
propagation.description: Learn the ground wave and ground reflection, height patterns, effective earth radius and radio horizon, radio ducts, knife-edge diffraction, ionospheric critical frequency and MUF, D-layer absorption, rain attenuation, and propagation models such as the Hata formula through multiple-choice questions.
propagation.intro:
Radio waves do more than travel in straight lines through free space. At low frequencies they travel along the ground as the ground wave, and on line-of-sight links the wave reflected from the ground interferes with the direct wave, so the field strength alternates with the receiving antenna height. The refractive index of the atmosphere decreases with height, so radio waves bend slightly toward the ground, which is handled with an effective earth radius. Layers where the refractive index changes steeply form radio ducts, and waves bend into the shadows of hills and buildings by diffraction.
HF waves are reflected by the ionosphere, and the upper limit of reflection is set by the critical frequency, determined by electron density, and by the secant law for the angle of incidence. On links above 10 GHz, rain attenuation dominates link design and is estimated from the specific attenuation and the effective path length. Urban path loss is predicted with empirical models based on measurements, such as the Hata formula, with attention to their range of validity.
